issues.legal_issue: The requirement to accompany a document with a true copy applies to the document presented for registration, not to a power of attorney relied on to execute it.
material_facts: A sale instrument was presented for registration by a person who had executed it under a registered power of attorney.
The original power of attorney was not available to that person, who had obtained a certified copy.
The dispute included whether the registration legislation required a true copy of the power of attorney.
issues.conclusion: The true-copy requirement applies to the instrument sought to be registered; it does not require a true copy of the power of attorney. The Court did not decide whether a true copy of the sale instrument had been produced in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Section 18A of the Registration Act requires a true copy of the document sought to be registered. Its purpose is to avoid delay in copying that document into the registration records, not to require copies of documents on which its execution is based. The Court relied on the provision’s text and the Statement of Objects and Reasons to the Punjab amendment from which it originated.

predicates.registration_requirement_dispute: The case concerns what document must be accompanied by a true copy when an instrument is presented for registration.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns the true-copy requirement in a registration proceeding, the required copy is of the instrument presented for registration.

issues.legal_issue: A person who executes an instrument as an attorney may present that instrument for registration as its executant without producing the original power of attorney for the registering officer’s inquiry.
material_facts: The attorney executed the sale instrument on the principal’s behalf and presented it for registration.
The attorney had a certified copy of the registered power of attorney, while the original was unavailable.
The challenge asserted that the original power of attorney had to be produced for valid presentation and registration.
issues.conclusion: The attorney, as the person who actually executed the instrument, could present it under Section 32(a). Sections 32(c), 33 and 34(3)(c), which concern an agent presenting a document on another person’s behalf, did not require production of the original power of attorney in these circumstances.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 32(a), 32(c), 33 and 34 of the Registration Act distinguish an actual executant from an agent authorised only to present a document. An attorney who executes the document is the executant for registration purposes and may present it under Section 32(a); the registering officer’s inquiry does not extend to whether that executant had a valid power to execute it. The Court applied Rajni Tandon v. Dulal Ranjan Ghosh Dastidar and referred to Jambu Prasad v. Muhammad Aftab Ali Khan on the need for presentation in accordance with law.

predicates.registration_dispute: The case concerns the validity of presenting an instrument for registration.
predicates.agent_executed_instrument: A person acting under an asserted authority personally executed the instrument on another person’s behalf.
predicates.agent_presented_instrument: The person who executed the instrument presented it for registration.

issues.definition: In a registration dispute, a person who executed an instrument on another’s behalf may present it as the executant without producing the original authority document for the registering officer’s inquiry.

issues.legal_issue: A High Court hearing a second appeal cannot displace concurrent factual findings by reappreciating the evidence when no proper basis for interference is established.
material_facts: The trial court and the first appellate court both rejected the claim that the sale authority had been cancelled before the sale.
The High Court reassessed the evidence and reversed those findings in a second appeal.
The first appellate court had not fully complied with the requirements for setting out points for determination.
issues.conclusion: The High Court overstepped the limits of its second-appeal jurisdiction by reappreciating the evidence and disturbing the lower courts’ findings.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Code of Civil Procedure confines second appeals to substantial questions of law; reappreciation of evidence is ordinarily a task for the first appellate court. The Court also noted the requirements of Order XLI Rule 31 of the Code but held that the first appellate court’s incomplete compliance did not justify the High Court’s reappraisal of the evidence.

predicates.second_appeal: The proceeding before the High Court is a second appeal.
predicates.concurrent_factual_findings: The trial court and first appellate court reached the same factual findings on the disputed matter.
predicates.high_court_reappraised_evidence: The High Court reassessed the evidence to replace the lower courts’ factual findings.

issues.definition: In a second appeal, when both lower courts made the same factual findings and the High Court reassesses the evidence to replace them, that interference is unwarranted.

issues.legal_issue: An asserted revocation of an agent’s authority does not defeat a transaction with a third party unless the revocation is established and its effect has reached the relevant person.
material_facts: The principal claimed that the agent had returned the power of attorney and that it had been cancelled before the sale.
The principal’s later letter to the agent referred to having given the power of attorney and asked the agent to pursue a buyer and send money, without mentioning its return or cancellation.
The agent later informed the principal that the sale had been made under the power of attorney.
The principal gave no notice of cancellation, and the evidence did not establish that the purchaser knew of the alleged cancellation.
issues.conclusion: The alleged cancellation was not established. In any event, the purchaser could not be treated as having knowledge of the alleged revocation, so the sale could not be set aside on that basis. The Court did not decide whether a registered power of attorney can be cancelled only by a registered instrument.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 201 and 207 of the Contract Act, an agency may be terminated by revocation, express or implied, subject to the exception in Section 202 for an agency coupled with an agent’s interest. Under Section 208, termination takes effect against the agent when it becomes known to the agent and against a third person when it becomes known to that person. The Court also relied on the explanation in Pollock and Mulla, The Indian Contract and Specific Relief Acts, that a third party dealing in good faith and without notice may remain protected by the agent’s apparent authority.

predicates.agency_authority_dispute: The dispute concerns whether an agent had authority when making a transaction for a principal.
predicates.revocation_not_established: The evidence does not establish that the principal revoked the agent’s authority before the transaction.
predicates.third_party_unaware_of_revocation: The third party to the transaction did not know of the alleged revocation.

issues.definition: When a dispute concerns an agent’s authority, the alleged revocation is not established, and the third party lacks knowledge of it, the transaction is not invalidated for lack of authority.

issues.legal_issue: An agent’s breach of a separate restriction on the minimum sale price does not, by itself, invalidate a sale made under a power of attorney that authorises the agent to sell at any price.
material_facts: The power of attorney authorised the agent to sell the property at whatever price the agent chose.
A separate agreement between the principal and the agent stated that the agent would sell only for a specified minimum price.
The agent sold the property for less than that minimum price.
The trial court found the agent bound by the separate agreement and liable to account to the principal.
issues.conclusion: Even assuming the agent breached the separate agreement by selling below the stipulated price, that breach could not invalidate the sale or make it void.
issues.legal_principle: The authority conferred by the power of attorney contained no minimum-price restriction. The separate agreement could bind the agent, but the agent’s breach of that obligation did not invalidate the conveyance. The Court relied on the terms of the power of attorney and the separate agreement; it cited no earlier case or statutory provision for this conclusion.

rule.if: sale_by_authorised_agent and broad_sale_authority and separate_minimum_price_restriction and sale_below_restriction

predicates.sale_by_authorised_agent: An agent makes a sale on behalf of a principal under an asserted authority.
predicates.broad_sale_authority: The authority document permits the agent to sell without imposing a minimum price.
predicates.separate_minimum_price_restriction: A separate agreement between the principal and agent restricts the price at which the agent may sell.
predicates.sale_below_restriction: The agent sells for less than the price required by the separate agreement.

issues.definition: When an agent sells under broad authority but breaches a separate minimum-price restriction, the breach alone does not make the sale void.
